title: Willey video can't go public, family told
article: The RCMP is suggesting the only way the video footage of the controversial in-custody treatment of Clayton Willey could be publicly released is with the permission of the dead man himself.
The police claimed came during a meeting Friday between senior RCMP officials and members of the Willey family, along with their supporters, in Vancouver.

RCMP offered in November to talk with them as Willey's family considered whether or not to ask the RCMP to release a video showing the 33-year-old man -- who was arrested and hogtied after a violent, drug-crazed altercation with several officers -- being dragged down a hallway; his head hitting an elevator; a Taser targeting his back; being dragged out of an elevator; and being Tasered twice more. Wiley would subsequently be taken from police custody by ambulance and go into cardiac arrest en route to then Prince George Regional Hospital; he died the next day and a 2004 coroner's inquest ruled the death was the result of a cocaine overdose.
RCMP had initially said that, if the family gave its approval, the video would be released.

But at the meeting, Grand Chief Stewart Phillip of the Union of B.C. Indian Chiefs (UBCIC), whose group is among those supporting the Willeys, said the police intimated that, even if the family asks for a release, privacy laws dictate that the only party that can OK putting the video into the public domain is the late Clayton Willey.

"Of course, the family wasn't thrilled to hear that and were quite upset," said Phillip, who added the meeting was "very intense and emotional." "The RCMP just kind of put its palms up and sort of said 'it's not our law, we don't make the laws.'" The claim also surprised Simon Wagstaffe, the family's lawyer.

"It doesn't sound likely, frankly," said Wagstaffe. "It would be a very curious piece of legislation if that were true." The RCMP also showed their copy of surveillance footage taken from the Prince George detachment on the day Willey was brought in.

The Willey family say the version of the tape they saw, in 2004, in the office of their then lawyer Dan Weatherly, showed Willey being pulled from a police SUV by a 'hobble', the rope of the hog tie, with his head hitting part of the vehicle and then the vehicle bay's concrete floor.
The video the family was shown on Friday in Vancouver did not show that part of Willey's handling.

"The footage that they have shows the police vehicle entering the bay and you see the passenger side and the officers just beginning to assemble, and just at the point of extraction the camera immediately flips over and you're only seeing the driver's side of the vehicle, which completely obscures the removal of Mr. Willey," said Phillip.

Police told the Willeys on Friday that they may have seen 'ghost images' in 2004 -- a suggestion the family denies. The camera that would have shown Willey being removed and his head hitting the frame of the vehicle and then the concrete -- details which were heard at the coroner's inquiry -- appears to have malfunctioned.

"At the inquest, (the recollection is) that particular camera angle is stuck, that is to say while the other cameras are moving on in time, that one is fixed where it is, which suggests, ordinarily, the camera has ceased to function as it ought to," said Wagstaffe. "There is the suggestion one of the shots from the other camera had gotten overlaid on the shot."

Regardless, what happened to the video is now part of an investigation into the Willey case and the broader question of Taser use by law enforcement now being conducted by the Commission for Public Complaints against the RCMP (CPC).

Wagstaffe learned at the meeting that there are also now two new Code of Conduct inquiries linked to the Willey case being conducted in respect to two officers as well as an investigation into the original investigation into case that was conducted by the Serious Crimes Unit.

It was also noted by the RCMP during the meeting, said Wagstaffe, that, when the ambulance was called to the Prince George detachment, it was "for the purpose of sedating this guy so they can put him in cells."
"It's only when the ambulance guys saw him that they said, 'This guys coming to the hospital,'" said Wagstaffe.
